title: Optimal incremental enumeration of the length-k subsequences of a word: linear preprocessing time and constant delay
author: Duncan Adamson, Pamela Fleischmann, Annika Huch, Florin Manea, Paul Sarnighausen-Cahn, Max Wiedenh\"oft
work: Tight Bounds for the Number of Absent Subsequences
difficulty_reason: The counted theorem is the main result of the article's algorithmic section and it is not a qualification exercise. With the article's earlier enumeration results supplied - Observation 1 on the next-occurrence and previous-occurrence arrays, Lemma 13 building the subsequence automaton and enumerating by depth-first traversal of the length-k paths, and Theorem 3 replacing the explicit automaton by range-minimum queries over the previous-occurrence array - the author still has to construct an optimal constant-delay incremental enumeration: the run-length arrays R and M, the jump-ahead and jump-back arrays with their two-case definition, the constant-time subroutine split with its two branches and its -1 case, the two stacks S and M carrying the succinct representation of the greedy embedding as maximal contiguous factors together with the beta flags that mark which records still have unenumerated continuations, and the induced update of both stacks in the two cases of empty and non-empty continuation queue. The mathematical content is the invariant that the simulated order of outputs is exactly the output order of the previous algorithm, together with the O(1) bound on the delay between consecutive outputs and the O(n) preprocessing bound, including the linear-time construction of the range-minimum structure over the previous-occurrence array. Designing and verifying an optimal-delay enumeration algorithm of this kind is research-level stringology and enumeration complexity, well beyond an ordinary PhD qualifying examination, even though the final correctness step is a refinement argument rather than a new structural theorem.
